# Was Microsoft Entra Connect Health hacked?

**Confirmed.** Yes, by Microsoft's own account: unauthorized parties exploited a flaw in the Connect Health API and read tenant metadata, including administrator emails. Who did it and how many were hit are not established.

Incident: Microsoft Entra Connect Health data exposure, Nov 2026. Also reported as Entra Connect Health breach and Microsoft Entra Connect Health flaw. First published Nov 21, 2026; last updated Nov 21, 2026, 1:17 PM ET.

Picture: Part of Microsoft's headquarters campus in Redmond, Washington. Image: Runner1928, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:View_of_Microsoft_campus_from_building_36.jpg).

> **Not verified: initial investigation only.** Nothing on this page is absolutely confirmed. It is an early look based only on publicly available sources, and it should not be treated as verified fact. Even items labeled "Confirmed" only mean a public source reports them. Made for entertainment using AI. Not endorsed by Microsoft, any news outlet, government agency, company, or anyone else named.

This is the current answer, not a final verdict.

## The latest

Nov 21, 2026, 1:17 PM ET: **Microsoft says attackers exploited a Connect Health flaw to read tenant metadata; who and how many are not established.** First draft. 6 sources (1 Tier 1, 2 Tier 2, 3 Tier 3), 15 claims (9 Confirmed, 1 Reported, 5 Not established), 9 questions. Microsoft says an Entra Connect Health API flaw, introduced Jul 23 and found Nov 9, let unauthorized parties read tenant-level metadata, including administrator emails, fixed server-side on Nov 19; it notified affected organizations on Nov 20. The label Confirmed records Microsoft's statements, relayed by two independent outlets and a Microsoft statement to one; we did not find the notification on a Microsoft page. Microsoft says no passwords, tokens or keys were exposed (its statement only). Attacker, affected count, start of exploitation, follow-on attacks and any link to other Microsoft incidents are Not established. No Reddit thread, leak site, dark-web page or tracker visited. Privacy check done: no names of officials, spokespeople or reporters, no handles, contact details or phone numbers.

## At a glance

- Status: monitoring
- Size: Large. A worldwide cloud service, but Microsoft has not said how many organizations were affected, so this size is a provisional estimate. More than a dozen administrators reported getting the notice, per one outlet's description of a social media thread.
- Who is affected: Organizations that received Microsoft's notice through Azure Service Health, per Microsoft. It says they need no software update, and advises watching for phishing aimed at exposed administrator emails.

| Value | What | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| Jul 23 | Flaw introduced | Per Microsoft's notification |
| Nov 19 | Server-side fix | Per Microsoft |
| Nov 20 | Investigation done, notices sent | Per Microsoft |

### Known so far

- Microsoft says unauthorized parties read tenant-level metadata through a flaw in the Entra Connect Health API.
- It says the flaw was introduced Jul 23 and discovered Nov 9.
- It says a server-side fix went live Nov 19 and no customer update is needed.
- It says it notified affected organizations on Nov 20.
- It says the exposed data included administrator and technical-contact emails and tenant configuration metadata.
- It says no passwords, tokens or valid keys were exposed (Microsoft's statement only).

### Not known yet

- Who exploited the flaw.
- How many organizations were affected.
- When unauthorized access began.
- Whether the exposed emails have been used in phishing.
- Whether Microsoft's statement that no passwords, tokens or keys were exposed holds up.

## What we checked and did not find

We looked for these and did not find them as of our latest check on Nov 21.

- A Microsoft security advisory, MSRC post or Learn page announcing the incident. The notification text reaches us only through outlets that quote it; the one Microsoft page we found is its GitHub page for the read-only reference scripts.
- A count of affected organizations, or any statement on when unauthorized access began.
- A published root cause beyond a vulnerability in the Connect Health API, or a post-incident report.
- Any named attacker, claim of responsibility, ransom or extortion claim, or published data reported by an outlet. We looked only at news coverage and Microsoft's pages. We did not visit leak sites, dark-web pages or trackers, and we did not read the Reddit thread outlets cite.
- Any report of phishing or other attacks that used the exposed emails or metadata.
- Any official or independent link to the Microsoft 365 outage or other Microsoft incidents.
- Any independent check of Microsoft's statements that no passwords, tokens or keys were exposed and that no configuration was changed.
